#### Reference issue

Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/15896

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

In short, this PR adds functionality to generate code coverage report C, C++ and Fortran code in SciPy. Basically achieves the two conditions mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#pullrequestreview-2449299817,

> 1. Run `lcov` in `python dev.py test` only when `--gcov` was enabled during SciPy build.
> 2. Exit without running tests only when any compiler than `gcc` was used to build SciPy and `--gcov` option was enabled. In all other cases run tests as it is.

See my reviews below for explanation behind the changes.

Describe your issue.

The documentation for the `func` parameter of `scipy.stats.sobol_indices` says

> If func is a dictionary, contains the function evaluations from three different arrays. Keys must be: `f_A`, `f_B` and `f_AB`. `f_A` and `f_B` should have a shape `(s, n)` and `f_AB` should have a shape `(d, s, n)`. This is an advanced feature and misuse can lead to wrong analysis.

I have incorporated this advanced feature of `scipy.stats.sobol_indices` in my analysis workflow. I observe that `scipy.stats.sobol_indices` modifies the values of the `func` dictionary in place. I do not imagine that this is the intended behavior. And if it is the intended behavior, then it needs to be documented, as it is unexpected.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import sobol_indices, uniform

def f_ishigami(x):
    f_eval = (
        np.sin(x[0])
        + 7 * np.sin(x[1])**2
        + 0.1 * (x[2]**4) * np.sin(x[0])
    )
    return f_eval

n = 4  # number of samples
d = 3  # input dimensionality
s = 1  # output dimensionality

np.random.seed(0)

foo = dict()
foo['A'] = uniform(loc=-np.pi, scale=2*np.pi).rvs((d, n))
foo['B'] = uniform(loc=-np.pi, scale=2*np.pi).rvs((d, n))
foo['AB'] = np.zeros(shape=(d, d, n))
for i in range(d):
    for j in range(n):
        foo['AB'][i, :, :] = foo['A'].copy()
        foo['AB'][i, i, :] = foo['B'][i, :].copy()

bar = dict()
bar['f_A'] = f_ishigami(foo['A']).reshape(s, n)
bar['f_B'] = f_ishigami(foo['B']).reshape(s, n)
bar['f_AB'] = f_ishigami(foo['AB']).reshape(d, s, n)

print('Before')
print(bar['f_A'])
print(bar['f_B'])
print(bar['f_AB'])
print()

indices = sobol_indices(func=bar, n=n)

print('After')
print(bar['f_A'])
print(bar['f_B'])
print(bar['f_AB'])
print()
```

> I will be working on it if somebody else is already not. Please let me know if anyone is already working on it, I will work on other issues then.
> Meanwhile, I am able to reproduce this bug. The modification happens in the following line (I commented these out and then the `bar` remains same before and after calling the function),
> https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/82ee02556872b9f91576b835a8f40f1d9eb1fd8d/scipy/stats/_sensitivity_analysis.py#L682-L684
> I guess we can just deepcopy `f_A`, `f_B`, `f_AB` in the following line,
> https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/82ee02556872b9f91576b835a8f40f1d9eb1fd8d/scipy/stats/_sensitivity_analysis.py#L667-L669
> I think `f_A`, `f_B`, `f_AB` are required to be mutated so deepcopying them from input dictionary is the only way I can think of to preserve the input arrays. Let me know if you there is a better way to achieve the same.

In short, this PR adds functionality to generate code coverage report C, C++ and Fortran code in SciPy. Basically achieves the two conditions mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#pullrequestreview-2449299817,

> 1. Run `lcov` in `python dev.py test` only when `--gcov` was enabled during SciPy build.
> 2. Exit without running tests only when any compiler than `gcc` was used to build SciPy and `--gcov` option was enabled. In all other cases run tests as it is.

See my reviews below for explanation behind the changes.

Steps to reproduce the change here and in https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238,

1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.

This came up when I was testing a greater change for these files via jupyterlite/jupyterlite-sphinx#221, so I thought it would be nice to fix what I noticed upstream with a quick PR until we roll out that feature and port it over here (should be soon).

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

- ed82988b4f358f1daeb0371f5d05b6cc17ad38d7 removes the usage of the Jupytext CLI being called, because we can use the Jupytext API directly. Further, even if we were to use the CLI and an API were not available, using `os.system("python3 <...>")` isn't really a good idea when we already have `subprocess.check_call([f"{sys.executable}])`.
- c5228f5a1d3ba7e1458aaeb68a2d9d7a75143256 drops the usage of [`os.path.getctime`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.path.html#os.path.getctime) for timestamp-based caching, because its behaviour is different across Unix and Windows:
     - Unix returns the last metadata change time, but Windows returns the creation time
     - We switch to [`os.stat().st_mtime`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.stat_result.st_mtime) instead because it's more consistent across platforms and directly measures what we care about here (the time between changes between the file contents across docs builds). We don't need to access the creation time for invalidating caches.
     - Also, this commit removes the equality expression from the check because it is an impossible condition to meet – one will modify the Markdown file(s) only after Jupytext has converted them.

drops the use of staged installs with `--destdir` in favor of using `--prefix` for the install location. The problem is that RPATHs in extension modules end up pointing to what Meson thinks is the final install location (i.e., inside the prefix) rather than to the staging directory.

`--destdir` seems meant for packaging, as an actual staging area, while for `spin` the final install directory is `build-install` (by default), there is no intent to later put this package into `/usr` or `C:\`. Hence using `--prefix` seems like the correct thing to do.

The one test change here is to a test that was incorrect. `meson setup --prefix` expects an absolute path, and `/foobar` isn't a path that exists or can be created.

Addresses the issue discussed in gh-238 - the `spin build` behavior before this change cannot be made to work for SciPy, because the internal shared library in `scipy.special` keeps breaking. It should also address the problem discussed in issue gh-176.

It may be my fault for suggesting the use of `--destdir` early on in `spin`'s life - I think I understand the tradeoffs a bit better now.

@stefanv question about testing - do you want me to extend `example_pkg` with a shared library? It will look like `sharedlib-in-package/mypkg/sub/*` in https://github.com/mesonbuild/meson-python/pull/700. 1. Firstly, if `spin build` is not executed before calling `spin test` then the build command is invoked inside `parent_callback` (effectively inside `spin`). Calling it on our own inside SciPy will be redundant. Now, [this piece of code](https://github.com/czgdp1807/scipy/blob/60a6d0390037c5ec4cd7ebb1fdbefcdfb4eff53e/.spin/cmds.py#L255-L274) requires SciPy to be already built (i.e., `spin build` must have been called already). Basically it checks which compiler was used to compile SciPy. If it is not compiled with `gcc` and `--gcov` was enabled during SciPy build, then tests aren't run. Reason is explained in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#discussion_r1850734770. Now, if SciPy is not already built then we don't know which compiler was used. So the user will face missing symbol error (see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#discussion_r1850734770) when they run the tests. We can't add my check linked above in `spin` because it is SciPy specific. For now @rgommers and I have decided to raise an error if `spin test --coverage` is called without calling `spin build` before. It is a must to make sure that users don't face test giving missing symbol error.
2. We can't execute code after call to `parent_callback` while extending `spin` commands. In other words, no code after `parent_callback` is executed. For now [I added `try-finally`](https://github.com/czgdp1807/scipy/blob/60a6d0390037c5ec4cd7ebb1fdbefcdfb4eff53e/.spin/cmds.py#L312-L317) block to run `lcov` once `parent_callback` is complete (`lcov` can only called after completion of test execution which is done by `parent_callback`).  I think we should be able to do this without `try-finally` block.

@stefanv Any thoughts on the above two observations?

I did my own analysis and found that refcount of `obj` is 2. So there is a memory leak indeed (or reference leak). Why? Because when the `thread_dict` will be destroyed then the refcount of `obj` will reduce to 1 (from 2). So there will be a leak. We should do `Py_DECREF(obj)` to ensure that there is only one reference of `obj` i.e., inside the `thread_dict`.

I applied the following diff to SciPy,

```diff
diff --git a/scipy/sparse/linalg/_dsolve/_superlu_utils.c b/scipy/sparse/linalg/_dsolve/_superlu_utils.c
index 49b928a43..a2bb82511 100644
--- a/scipy/sparse/linalg/_dsolve/_superlu_utils.c
+++ b/scipy/sparse/linalg/_dsolve/_superlu_utils.c
@@ -27,6 +27,16 @@ static SuperLUGlobalObject *get_tls_global(void)
     }
     return &superlu_py_global;
 #else
+
+    #define printrefcnt(op)                                                     \
+        do {                                                                     \
+            PyObject *__p = (PyObject*) op;                                                   \
+            printf("scipy/sparse/linalg/_dsolve/_superlu_utils.c:%d %s:%d refcnt(%s:0x%lx) = %ld\n", __LINE__, \
+                __PRETTY_FUNCTION__, __LINE__, \
+                #op, (uintptr_t)__p, Py_REFCNT(__p));                            \
+        } while (0);
+

Same code and diff as in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/16234#issuecomment-2533817282

`tmpobj` is not needed after `trans_cvt`, its an argument processing function I think. So, setting reference count of `tmpobj` to `0` should be safe. That should fix the memory leak also. `tmpobj` is converted to `s` via `PyBytes_AS_STRING`. After this, `tmpobj` can be garbage collected safely because whatever we need is now in `s`. I can set it to `1` but `4294967295` (basically `-1`, since its stored in unsigned type so that's why its such a large number). However, that would leak memory because `tmpobj` is not needed after we have `s`.

Would like to what other folks think on it.

#### Reference issue

Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/16009

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

Note that `act -v -j test_meson` won't work because there are multiple jobs with same name in more than one workflow file. For example, `test_meson` is in `linux.yml` and `macos.yml`. So `act` launches both and hence it launches `docker` containers with same name for both the jobs and hence fails at that point. This I think is a `act` level issue. See the message shown by `act`,

```
.
.
.
Detected multiple jobs with the same job name, use `-W` to specify the path to the specific workflow.
```

One needs to do `act -v -j test_meson -W .github/workflows/linux.yml`.

Describe your issue.

While writing a cpp wrapper for scipy, the following warning was shown due to the very old Fortran coding style used in the fitpack part in interpolation.
```
interpolate/fitpack/*.f
```

Warning: Fortran 2018 deleted feature: Shared DO termination

This can easily be solved. E.g.:

```
      do 20 i=1,k1
         t(i) = xb
         t(j) = xe
         j = j-1
  20  continue
  ```
  
must be changed to 

```
      do i=1,k1
         t(i) = xb
         t(j) = xe
         j = j-1
      end do
```


### Reproducing Code Example

```python
none
```


### Error message

```shell
Warning: Warning: Fortran 2018 deleted feature: Shared DO termination
```

Describe your issue.

According to the documentation, RectBivariateSpline can be used for smoothing by setting `s` to a non zero value. This works on small grids, but on larger grids, using any `s` value other than zero produces a spline that evaluates to NaN everywhere. To be clear, this occurs on data that do not contain any NaN. The problem occurs without any warning or error message. The problem occurs irregularly (running the code sometimes work, but most of the time it does not).

The problem occurs on grid with dtype int as well as float.

The problem occurs on Windows 10 and mac OS.

Since the problem does not alway occur, I suspect it may be due to a failure to allocate memory. If enough memory is available, everything works fine. However, it the memory allocation fails, RectBivariateSpline returns a nonsensical result without informing the user about the memory error.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import interpolate

s = 1  # any value greater than zero causes the problem
nx, ny = 1000, 1700    # Set to larger values to reproduce the problem more consistently
img = np.random.randint(0, 100, size=(nx, ny))
x = np.arange(nx)
y = np.arange(ny)
spl = interpolate.RectBivariateSpline(x, y, img, s=s)
print(np.isnan(spl(x, y)).any())
```


### Error message

```shell
No error message
```

this PR I would first implement a `simplifier` pass which would contain all the logic just for creating auxiliaries for expressions which need them. Allocatables to be only created when there is no possibility of creating a fixed size array. 

`simplifier` pass would also contain a verifier inside it which would check the output ASR satisfies constraints and if not then compilation should stop right there without moving to other passes. This way bugs won't reach the LLVM backend and we will have easier time debugging. 

Right now we apply `array_op`, `subroutine_from_function` more than once which I don't like. After `simplifier`, all those double application of the same pass should be removed entirely. Also `array_op`, `subroutine_from_function`, `intrinsic_function`, `init_expr` all have their separate codes for creating temporary variables (which are sometimes allocatables). So lots of bugs present in all these passes. After `simplifier` pass, these 4-5 passes I mentioned won't create any new variable or allocatables, they would just replace expressions like `Var` with `ArrayItem`. Nothing else. This way, these passes would speed up and we won't be required to track bugs down in different passes. Only `simplifier` would required to be dealt with.

This refactoring would allow us to compile larger codes with greater ease. I will also make sure to allow for optimisations for nodes like `ImpliedDoLoop` in the `simplifier` pass. This would keep the doors open for the future. For now correctness and management of the code matters the most. I have seen lots of problems with temporary variables, auxiliaries while compiling `stdlib`. Sometimes the bugs pass on silently to the LLVM backend and until then its too late. I would make sure that `simplifier` pass catches the bugs early on (even if miss out some nodes then the error is raised right there instead of just passing ahead to other passes Introduction
Rebase, reorganization, and code review of [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019).

#### Original description
Another pull request to speed up sparse.csgraph.dijkstra, succeeding https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/16696
Thank you @jjerphan for reviewing the previous pull request and giving me advice

* Replaces FibonacciHeap with std::priority_queue which makes sparse.csgraph.dijkstra faster
   * asymptotically due to the removal of a bug in FibonacciHeap implementation
   * with regard to the constant factor due to better memory usage(?)
* Unifies the four similar dijkstra functions into one
   * Performance overhead was negligible, probably because the priority_queue is the bottleneck
* Adds the star graph to the benchmark as the worst case for the previous version
* Fixes a typo in the test file name
* A part of the test file for dijkstra is modified for better readability, nothing really changed
( See benchmarks in [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019)).

### Changes from original PR
* Squashed tiny commits into larger commits (e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/90b5151b766f8d68c74fa0f8b5ca6ecd62eb7bf5)).
* Removing irrelevant commits due to changes in repo since the original PR was opened ( e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/92b53181f1fcdb90ec8d3ef2285195e2271c2d55) one).
* Adapted Yen's algorithm to the new Dijkstra internal implementation (under [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/commit/24fddcd7f7d0e8bf65724583515f86361266e7ff) commit).
* Removed random testing ( as I agree with the comment [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17800#pullrequestreview-1251442515)), instead added a star-graph test.

```python
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import shortest_path
import numpy as np, scipy, timeit, functools
from tabulate import tabulate

def scipy_dijkstra(graph):
    shortest_path(graph, method='D', directed=False)

p_m = u" \u00B1 "
mu = u" \u03BC "
sigma = u" \u03C3 "
results = []
densities = [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.9]
for density in densities:
    result = [density]
    result.append('Dijkstra')
    A = (scipy.sparse.rand(1000, 1000, density, format='csr')*100).astype(np.uint32)
    t = timeit.Timer(functools.partial(scipy_dijkstra, A))
    times = t.repeat(3, 1)
    result.append(str(np.mean(times).round(3)) + p_m + str(np.std(times).round(3)))

    results.append(result)

print(tabulate(results, headers=[
    'Density', 'Algorithm',
    mu + p_m + sigma],
    tablefmt='github'), end="\n\n")
```

This PR gives significant performance gains,

On `main` branch,

```
|   Density | Algorithm   |  μ  ±  σ      |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|
|       0.1 | Dijkstra    | 0.985 ± 0.016 |
|       0.3 | Dijkstra    | 2.321 ± 0.006 |
|       0.5 | Dijkstra    | 3.801 ± 0.032 |
|       0.9 | Dijkstra    | 5.748 ± 0.073 |
```

On this PR,

```
|   Density | Algorithm   |  μ  ±  σ      |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|
|       0.1 | Dijkstra    | 0.636 ± 0.002 |
|       0.3 | Dijkstra    | 0.938 ± 0.002 |
|       0.5 | Dijkstra    | 1.267 ± 0.009 |
|       0.9 | Dijkstra    | 1.944 ± 0.009 |
```

I can't go more than 1000 x 1000 because `main` branch hangs with sizes above 1000 x 1000.

Introduction
Rebase, reorganization, and code review of [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019).

#### Original description
Another pull request to speed up sparse.csgraph.dijkstra, succeeding https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/16696
Thank you @jjerphan for reviewing the previous pull request and giving me advice

* Replaces FibonacciHeap with std::priority_queue which makes sparse.csgraph.dijkstra faster
   * asymptotically due to the removal of a bug in FibonacciHeap implementation
   * with regard to the constant factor due to better memory usage(?)
* Unifies the four similar dijkstra functions into one
   * Performance overhead was negligible, probably because the priority_queue is the bottleneck
* Adds the star graph to the benchmark as the worst case for the previous version
* Fixes a typo in the test file name
* A part of the test file for dijkstra is modified for better readability, nothing really changed
( See benchmarks in [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019)).

### Changes from original PR
* Squashed tiny commits into larger commits (e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/90b5151b766f8d68c74fa0f8b5ca6ecd62eb7bf5)).
* Removing irrelevant commits due to changes in repo since the original PR was opened ( e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/92b53181f1fcdb90ec8d3ef2285195e2271c2d55) one).
* Adapted Yen's algorithm to the new Dijkstra internal implementation (under [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/commit/24fddcd7f7d0e8bf65724583515f86361266e7ff) commit).
* Removed random testing ( as I agree with the comment [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17800#pullrequestreview-1251442515)), instead added a star-graph test.

Another pull request to speed up sparse.csgraph.dijkstra, succeeding https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/16696
Thank you @jjerphan for reviewing the previous pull request and giving me advice

* Replaces FibonacciHeap with std::priority_queue which makes sparse.csgraph.dijkstra faster
   * asymptotically due to the removal of a bug in FibonacciHeap implementation
   * with regard to the constant factor due to better memory usage(?)
* Unifies the four similar dijkstra functions into one
   * Performance overhead was negligible, probably because the priority_queue is the bottleneck
* Adds the star graph to the benchmark as the worst case for the previous version
* Fixes a typo in the test file name
* A part of the test file for dijkstra is modified for better readability, nothing really changed
( See benchmarks in [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019)).

### Changes from original PR
* Squashed tiny commits into larger commits (e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/90b5151b766f8d68c74fa0f8b5ca6ecd62eb7bf5)).
* Removing irrelevant commits due to changes in repo since the original PR was opened ( e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/92b53181f1fcdb90ec8d3ef2285195e2271c2d55) one).
* Adapted Yen's algorithm to the new Dijkstra internal implementation (under [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/commit/24fddcd7f7d0e8bf65724583515f86361266e7ff) commit).
* Removed random testing ( as I agree with the comment [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17800#pullrequestreview-1251442515)), instead added a star-graph test.

Rebase, reorganization, and code review of [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019).

#### Original description
Another pull request to speed up sparse.csgraph.dijkstra, succeeding https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/16696
Thank you @jjerphan for reviewing the previous pull request and giving me advice

* Replaces FibonacciHeap with std::priority_queue which makes sparse.csgraph.dijkstra faster
   * asymptotically due to the removal of a bug in FibonacciHeap implementation
   * with regard to the constant factor due to better memory usage(?)
* Unifies the four similar dijkstra functions into one
   * Performance overhead was negligible, probably because the priority_queue is the bottleneck
* Adds the star graph to the benchmark as the worst case for the previous version
* Fixes a typo in the test file name
* A part of the test file for dijkstra is modified for better readability, nothing really changed
( See benchmarks in [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019)).

### Changes from original PR
* Squashed tiny commits into larger commits (e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/90b5151b766f8d68c74fa0f8b5ca6ecd62eb7bf5)).
* Removing irrelevant commits due to changes in repo since the original PR was opened ( e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/92b53181f1fcdb90ec8d3ef2285195e2271c2d55) one).
* Adapted Yen's algorithm to the new Dijkstra internal implementation (under [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/commit/24fddcd7f7d0e8bf65724583515f86361266e7ff) commit).
* Removed random testing ( as I agree with the comment [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17800#pullrequestreview-1251442515)), instead added a star-graph test.

Introduction
Rebase, reorganization, and code review of [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019).

#### Original description
Another pull request to speed up sparse.csgraph.dijkstra, succeeding https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/16696
Thank you @jjerphan for reviewing the previous pull request and giving me advice

* Replaces FibonacciHeap with std::priority_queue which makes sparse.csgraph.dijkstra faster
   * asymptotically due to the removal of a bug in FibonacciHeap implementation
   * with regard to the constant factor due to better memory usage(?)
* Unifies the four similar dijkstra functions into one
   * Performance overhead was negligible, probably because the priority_queue is the bottleneck
* Adds the star graph to the benchmark as the worst case for the previous version
* Fixes a typo in the test file name
* A part of the test file for dijkstra is modified for better readability, nothing really changed
( See benchmarks in [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019)).

### Changes from original PR
* Squashed tiny commits into larger commits (e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/90b5151b766f8d68c74fa0f8b5ca6ecd62eb7bf5)).
* Removing irrelevant commits due to changes in repo since the original PR was opened ( e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/92b53181f1fcdb90ec8d3ef2285195e2271c2d55) one).
* Adapted Yen's algorithm to the new Dijkstra internal implementation (under [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/commit/24fddcd7f7d0e8bf65724583515f86361266e7ff) commit).
* Removed random testing ( as I agree with the comment [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17800#pullrequestreview-1251442515)), instead added a star-graph test.

Introduction
Rebase, reorganization, and code review of [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019).

#### Original description
Another pull request to speed up sparse.csgraph.dijkstra, succeeding https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/16696
Thank you @jjerphan for reviewing the previous pull request and giving me advice

* Replaces FibonacciHeap with std::priority_queue which makes sparse.csgraph.dijkstra faster
   * asymptotically due to the removal of a bug in FibonacciHeap implementation
   * with regard to the constant factor due to better memory usage(?)
* Unifies the four similar dijkstra functions into one
   * Performance overhead was negligible, probably because the priority_queue is the bottleneck
* Adds the star graph to the benchmark as the worst case for the previous version
* Fixes a typo in the test file name
* A part of the test file for dijkstra is modified for better readability, nothing really changed
( See benchmarks in [PR 17019](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019)).

### Changes from original PR
* Squashed tiny commits into larger commits (e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/90b5151b766f8d68c74fa0f8b5ca6ecd62eb7bf5)).
* Removing irrelevant commits due to changes in repo since the original PR was opened ( e.g., [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17019/commits/92b53181f1fcdb90ec8d3ef2285195e2271c2d55) one).
* Adapted Yen's algorithm to the new Dijkstra internal implementation (under [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/commit/24fddcd7f7d0e8bf65724583515f86361266e7ff) commit).
* Removed random testing ( as I agree with the comment [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17800#pullrequestreview-1251442515)), instead added a star-graph test.

Describe your issue.

According to the documentation, RectBivariateSpline can be used for smoothing by setting `s` to a non zero value. This works on small grids, but on larger grids, using any `s` value other than zero produces a spline that evaluates to NaN everywhere. To be clear, this occurs on data that do not contain any NaN. The problem occurs without any warning or error message. The problem occurs irregularly (running the code sometimes work, but most of the time it does not).

The problem occurs on grid with dtype int as well as float.

The problem occurs on Windows 10 and mac OS.

Since the problem does not alway occur, I suspect it may be due to a failure to allocate memory. If enough memory is available, everything works fine. However, it the memory allocation fails, RectBivariateSpline returns a nonsensical result without informing the user about the memory error.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import interpolate

s = 1  # any value greater than zero causes the problem
nx, ny = 1000, 1700    # Set to larger values to reproduce the problem more consistently
img = np.random.randint(0, 100, size=(nx, ny))
x = np.arange(nx)
y = np.arange(ny)
spl = interpolate.RectBivariateSpline(x, y, img, s=s)
print(np.isnan(spl(x, y)).any())
```


### Error message

```shell
No error message
```

Describe your issue.

According to the documentation, RectBivariateSpline can be used for smoothing by setting `s` to a non zero value. This works on small grids, but on larger grids, using any `s` value other than zero produces a spline that evaluates to NaN everywhere. To be clear, this occurs on data that do not contain any NaN. The problem occurs without any warning or error message. The problem occurs irregularly (running the code sometimes work, but most of the time it does not).

The problem occurs on grid with dtype int as well as float.

The problem occurs on Windows 10 and mac OS.

Since the problem does not alway occur, I suspect it may be due to a failure to allocate memory. If enough memory is available, everything works fine. However, it the memory allocation fails, RectBivariateSpline returns a nonsensical result without informing the user about the memory error.

import numpy as np

x = np.arange(nx)
y = np.arange(ny)
spl = interpolate.RectBivariateSpline(x, y, img, s=s)
print(np.isnan(spl(x, y)).any())
```

No error message

For things like `x = f(a)`, we need to go into the function signature, and extract the dimension of the result as an expression / function of the arguments, and then substitute using the actual arguments in the expression. 

So in the end we end up with each node in the array expression having an expression for each dimension as a function of the parent variables in the expression, and it does *not* call any user function. 

The simplifier pass can then take these expressions and allocate a temporary array on stack, as needed.

Your change is better (it is backwards compatible), however since `--prefix=/usr` doesn't work with SciPy, so we will have to pass `--prefix=<abs_install_dir>` in SciPy project. 

Basically the choice to be made here is,

1. Option 1 - Follow https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/241/files and pass `--prefix=<abs_build_dir>`.
2. Option 2 - Follow this PR (once it's merged in `main` branch of `spin`). Then NumPy and SciPy will work fine as is. However, its hard to say if other projects using `spin` will break or not.

I am fine with Option 1. That way only SciPy interface will need changes and no other project using spin will break.

In SciPy each step i.e., `compile`, `setup` and `install` needs arguments from `meson_args`. You can't pass everything from `meson_args` tuple directly into the first command. So I added 3 keys, `"compile"`, `"setup"` and `"install"` to differentiate which meson argument from SciPy to pass in which step.

+def configure_scipy_openblas(self, blas_variant='32'):
+    """Create scipy-openblas.pc and scipy/_distributor_init_local.py
+
+    Requires a pre-installed scipy-openblas32 wheel from PyPI.
+    """
+    basedir = os.getcwd()
+    pkg_config_fname = os.path.join(basedir, "scipy-openblas.pc")
+
+    if os.path.exists(pkg_config_fname):
+        return None
+
+    module_name = f"scipy_openblas{blas_variant}"
+    try:
+        openblas = importlib.import_module(module_name)
+    except ModuleNotFoundError:
+        raise RuntimeError(f"Importing '{module_name}' failed. "
+                            "Make sure it is installed and reachable "
+                            "by the current Python executable. You can "
+                            f"install it via 'pip install {module_name}'.")
+
+    local = os.path.join(basedir, "scipy", "_distributor_init_local.py")
+    with open(local, "w", encoding="utf8") as fid:
+        fid.write(f"import {module_name}\n")
+
+    with open(pkg_config_fname, "w", encoding="utf8") as fid:
+        fid.write(openblas.get_pkg_config())

+physical_cores_cache = None

+def _cpu_count_cgroup(os_cpu_count):
+    # Cgroup CPU bandwidth limit available in Linux since 2.6 kernel
+    cpu_max_fname = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max"
+    cfs_quota_fname = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us"
+    cfs_period_fname = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us"
+    if os.path.exists(cpu_max_fname):
+        # cgroup v2
+        # https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html
+        with open(cpu_max_fname) as fh:
+            cpu_quota_us, cpu_period_us = fh.read().strip().split()
+    elif os.path.exists(cfs_quota_fname) and os.path.exists(cfs_period_fname):
+        # cgroup v1
+        # https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/scheduler/sched-bwc.html#management
+        with open(cfs_quota_fname) as fh:
+            cpu_quota_us = fh.read().strip()
+        with open(cfs_period_fname) as fh:
+            cpu_period_us = fh.read().strip()
+    else:
+        # No Cgroup CPU bandwidth limit (e.g. non-Linux platform)
+        cpu_quota_us = "max"
+        cpu_period_us = 100_000  # unused, for consistency with default values
+
+    if cpu_quota_us == "max":
+        # No active Cgroup quota on a Cgroup-capable platform
+        return os_cpu_count
+    else:
+        cpu_quota_us = int(cpu_quota_us)
+        cpu_period_us = int(cpu_period_us)
+        if cpu_quota_us > 0 and cpu_period_us > 0:
+            return math.ceil(cpu_quota_us / cpu_period_us)
+        else:  # pragma: no cover
+            # Setting a negative cpu_quota_us value is a valid way to disable
+            # cgroup CPU bandwidth limits
+            return os_cpu_count
+
+
+def _cpu_count_affinity(os_cpu_count):
+    # Number of available CPUs given affinity settings
+    if hasattr(os, "sched_getaffinity"):
+        try:
+            return len(os.sched_getaffinity(0))
+        except NotImplementedError:
+            pass
+
+    # On PyPy and possibly other platforms, os.sched_getaffinity does not exist
+    # or raises NotImplementedError, let's try with the psutil if installed.
+    try:
+        import psutil
+
+        p = psutil.Process()
+        if hasattr(p, "cpu_affinity"):
+            return len(p.cpu_affinity())
+
+    except ImportError:  # pragma: no cover
+        if (
+            sys.platform == "linux"
+            and os.environ.get("LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT") is None
+        ):
+            # PyPy does not implement os.sched_getaffinity on Linux which
+            # can cause severe oversubscription problems. Better warn the
+            # user in this particularly pathological case which can wreck
+            # havoc, typically on CI workers.
+            warnings.warn(
+                "Failed to inspect CPU affinity constraints on this system. "
+                "Please install psutil or explicitly set LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT.",
+                stacklevel=4
+            )
+
+    # This can happen for platforms that do not implement any kind of CPU
+    # infinity such as macOS-based platforms.
+    return os_cpu_count
+
+
+def _cpu_count_user(os_cpu_count):
+    """Number of user defined available CPUs"""
+    cpu_count_affinity = _cpu_count_affinity(os_cpu_count)
+
+    cpu_count_cgroup = _cpu_count_cgroup(os_cpu_count)
+
+    # User defined soft-limit passed as a loky specific environment variable.
+    cpu_count_loky = int(os.environ.get("LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT", os_cpu_count))
+
+    return min(cpu_count_affinity, cpu_count_cgroup, cpu_count_loky)
+
+def _count_physical_cores():
+    """Return a tuple (number of physical cores, exception)
+
+    If the number of physical cores is found, exception is set to None.
+    If it has not been found, return ("not found", exception).
+
+    The number of physical cores is cached to avoid repeating subprocess calls.
+    """
+    exception = None
+
+    # First check if the value is cached
+    global physical_cores_cache
+    if physical_cores_cache is not None:
+        return physical_cores_cache, exception
+
+    # Not cached yet, find it
+    try:
+        if sys.platform == "linux":
+            cpu_info = subprocess.run(
+                "lscpu --parse=core".split(), capture_output=True, text=True
+            )
+            cpu_info = cpu_info.stdout.splitlines()
+            cpu_info = {line for line in cpu_info if not line.startswith("#")}
+            cpu_count_physical = len(cpu_info)
+        elif sys.platform == "win32":
+            cpu_info = subprocess.run(
+                "wmic CPU Get NumberOfCores /Format:csv".split(),
+                capture_output=True,
+                text=True,
+            )
+            cpu_info = cpu_info.stdout.splitlines()
+            cpu_info = [
+                l.split(",")[1]
+                for l in cpu_info
+                if (l and l != "Node,NumberOfCores")
+            ]
+            cpu_count_physical = sum(map(int, cpu_info))
+        elif sys.platform == "darwin":
+            cpu_info = subprocess.run(
+                "sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu".split(),
+                capture_output=True,
+                text=True,
+            )
+            cpu_info = cpu_info.stdout
+            cpu_count_physical = int(cpu_info)
+        else:
+            raise NotImplementedError(f"unsupported platform: {sys.platform}")
+
+        # if cpu_count_physical < 1, we did not find a valid value
+        if cpu_count_physical < 1:
+            raise ValueError(f"found {cpu_count_physical} physical cores < 1")
+
+    except Exception as e:
+        exception = e
+        cpu_count_physical = "not found"
+
+    # Put the result in cache
+    physical_cores_cache = cpu_count_physical
+
+    return cpu_count_physical, exception
+
+def cpu_count(only_physical_cores=False):
+    """Return the number of CPUs the current process can use.
+
+    The returned number of CPUs accounts for:
+     * the number of CPUs in the system, as given by
+       ``multiprocessing.cpu_count``;
+     * the CPU affinity settings of the current process
+       (available on some Unix systems);
+     * Cgroup CPU bandwidth limit (available on Linux only, typically
+       set by docker and similar container orchestration systems);
+     * the value of the LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT environment variable if defined.
+    and is given as the minimum of these constraints.
+
+    If ``only_physical_cores`` is True, return the number of physical cores
+    instead of the number of logical cores (hyperthreading / SMT). Note that
+    this option is not enforced if the number of usable cores is controlled in
+    any other way such as: process affinity, Cgroup restricted CPU bandwidth
+    or the LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT environment variable. If the number of physical
+    cores is not found, return the number of logical cores.
+
+    Note that on Windows, the returned number of CPUs cannot exceed 61 (or 60 for
+    Python < 3.10), see:
+    https://bugs.python.org/issue26903.
+
+    It is also always larger or equal to 1.
+    """
+    # Note: os.cpu_count() is allowed to return None in its docstring
+    os_cpu_count = os.cpu_count() or 1
+    if sys.platform == "win32":
+        # On Windows, attempting to use more than 61 CPUs would result in a
+        # OS-level error. See https://bugs.python.org/issue26903. According to
+        # https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/processor-groups
+        # it might be possible to go beyond with a lot of extra work but this
+        # does not look easy.
+        os_cpu_count = min(os_cpu_count, _MAX_WINDOWS_WORKERS)
+
+    cpu_count_user = _cpu_count_user(os_cpu_count)
+    aggregate_cpu_count = max(min(os_cpu_count, cpu_count_user), 1)
+
+    if not only_physical_cores:
+        return aggregate_cpu_count
+
+    if cpu_count_user < os_cpu_count:
+        # Respect user setting
+        return max(cpu_count_user, 1)
+
+    cpu_count_physical, exception = _count_physical_cores()
+    if cpu_count_physical != "not found":
+        return cpu_count_physical
+
+    # Fallback to default behavior
+    if exception is not None:
+        # warns only the first time
+        warnings.warn(
+            "Could not find the number of physical cores for the "
+            f"following reason:\n{exception}\n"
+            "Returning the number of logical cores instead. You can "
+            "silence this warning by setting LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT to "
+            "the number of cores you want to use.",
+            stacklevel=2
+        )
+        traceback.print_tb(exception.__traceback__)
+
+    return aggregate_cpu_count

+                            "by the current Python executable. You can "
+                            f"install it via 'pip install {module_name}'.")

+    with open(local, "w", encoding="utf8") as fid:

+def _cpu_count_cgroup(os_cpu_count):
+    # Cgroup CPU bandwidth limit available in Linux since 2.6 kernel
+    cpu_max_fname = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max"
+    cfs_quota_fname = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us"
+    cfs_period_fname = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us"
+    if os.path.exists(cpu_max_fname):
+        # cgroup v2
+        # https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html
+        with open(cpu_max_fname) as fh:
+            cpu_quota_us, cpu_period_us = fh.read().strip().split()
+    elif os.path.exists(cfs_quota_fname) and os.path.exists(cfs_period_fname):
+        # cgroup v1
+        # https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/scheduler/sched-bwc.html#management
+        with open(cfs_quota_fname) as fh:
+            cpu_quota_us = fh.read().strip()
+        with open(cfs_period_fname) as fh:
+            cpu_period_us = fh.read().strip()
+    else:
+        # No Cgroup CPU bandwidth limit (e.g. non-Linux platform)
+        cpu_quota_us = "max"
+        cpu_period_us = 100_000  # unused, for consistency with default values
+
+    if cpu_quota_us == "max":
+        # No active Cgroup quota on a Cgroup-capable platform
+        return os_cpu_count
+    else:
+        cpu_quota_us = int(cpu_quota_us)
+        cpu_period_us = int(cpu_period_us)
+        if cpu_quota_us > 0 and cpu_period_us > 0:
+            return math.ceil(cpu_quota_us / cpu_period_us)
+        else:  # pragma: no cover
+            # Setting a negative cpu_quota_us value is a valid way to disable
+            # cgroup CPU bandwidth limits
+            return os_cpu_count

+def _cpu_count_affinity(os_cpu_count):
+    # Number of available CPUs given affinity settings
+    if hasattr(os, "sched_getaffinity"):
+        try:
+            return len(os.sched_getaffinity(0))
+        except NotImplementedError:
+            pass
+
+    # On PyPy and possibly other platforms, os.sched_getaffinity does not exist
+    # or raises NotImplementedError, let's try with the psutil if installed.
+    try:
+        import psutil
+
+        p = psutil.Process()
+        if hasattr(p, "cpu_affinity"):
+            return len(p.cpu_affinity())

+    except ImportError:  # pragma: no cover
+        if (
+            sys.platform == "linux"
+            and os.environ.get("LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT") is None

+            # can cause severe oversubscription problems. Better warn the
+            # user in this particularly pathological case which can wreck

+    # infinity such as macOS-based platforms.
+    return os_cpu_count

+def _cpu_count_user(os_cpu_count):
+    """Number of user defined available CPUs"""
+    cpu_count_affinity = _cpu_count_affinity(os_cpu_count)
+
+    cpu_count_cgroup = _cpu_count_cgroup(os_cpu_count)
+

+    cpu_count_loky = int(os.environ.get("LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT", os_cpu_count))
+
+    return min(cpu_count_affinity, cpu_count_cgroup, cpu_count_loky)

+def _count_physical_cores():
+    """Return a tuple (number of physical cores, exception)
+
+    If the number of physical cores is found, exception is set to None.
+    If it has not been found, return ("not found", exception).
+
+    The number of physical cores is cached to avoid repeating subprocess calls.
+    """
+    exception = None
+
+    # First check if the value is cached
+    global physical_cores_cache
+    if physical_cores_cache is not None:
+        return physical_cores_cache, exception
+
+    # Not cached yet, find it
+    try:
+        if sys.platform == "linux":
+            cpu_info = subprocess.run(
+                "lscpu --parse=core".split(), capture_output=True, text=True
+            )
+            cpu_info = cpu_info.stdout.splitlines()
+            cpu_info = {line for line in cpu_info if not line.startswith("#")}
+            cpu_count_physical = len(cpu_info)
+        elif sys.platform == "win32":
+            cpu_info = subprocess.run(
+                "wmic CPU Get NumberOfCores /Format:csv".split(),
+                capture_output=True,
+                text=True,
+            )
+            cpu_info = cpu_info.stdout.splitlines()
+            cpu_info = [
+                l.split(",")[1]
+                for l in cpu_info
+                if (l and l != "Node,NumberOfCores")
+            ]
+            cpu_count_physical = sum(map(int, cpu_info))
+        elif sys.platform == "darwin":
+            cpu_info = subprocess.run(
+                "sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu".split(),
+                capture_output=True,
+                text=True,

+
+    except Exception as e:
+        exception = e
+        cpu_count_physical = "not found"
+
+    # Put the result in cache
+    physical_cores_cache = cpu_count_physical
+
+    return cpu_count_physical, exception

+def cpu_count(only_physical_cores=False):
+    """Return the number of CPUs the current process can use.
+
+    The returned number of CPUs accounts for:
+     * the number of CPUs in the system, as given by
+       ``multiprocessing.cpu_count``;
+     * the CPU affinity settings of the current process
+       (available on some Unix systems);
+     * Cgroup CPU bandwidth limit (available on Linux only, typically
+       set by docker and similar container orchestration systems);
+     * the value of the LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT environment variable if defined.
+    and is given as the minimum of these constraints.
+
+    If ``only_physical_cores`` is True, return the number of physical cores
+    instead of the number of logical cores (hyperthreading / SMT). Note that
+    this option is not enforced if the number of usable cores is controlled in
+    any other way such as: process affinity, Cgroup restricted CPU bandwidth
+    or the LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT environment variable. If the number of physical
+    cores is not found, return the number of logical cores.
+
+    Note that on Windows, the returned number of CPUs cannot exceed 61 (or 60 for
+    Python < 3.10), see:
+    https://bugs.python.org/issue26903.
+
+    It is also always larger or equal to 1.

+    # Note: os.cpu_count() is allowed to return None in its docstring
+    os_cpu_count = os.cpu_count() or 1
+    if sys.platform == "win32":
+        # On Windows, attempting to use more than 61 CPUs would result in a
+        # OS-level error. See https://bugs.python.org/issue26903. According to
+        # https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/processor-groups
+        # it might be possible to go beyond with a lot of extra work but this
+        # does not look easy.
+        os_cpu_count = min(os_cpu_count, _MAX_WINDOWS_WORKERS)
+
+    cpu_count_user = _cpu_count_user(os_cpu_count)
+    aggregate_cpu_count = max(min(os_cpu_count, cpu_count_user), 1)
+
+    if not only_physical_cores:
+        return aggregate_cpu_count
+
+    if cpu_count_user < os_cpu_count:
+        # Respect user setting
+        return max(cpu_count_user, 1)
+
+    cpu_count_physical, exception = _count_physical_cores()
+    if cpu_count_physical != "not found":
+        return cpu_count_physical
+
+    # Fallback to default behavior
+    if exception is not None:
+        # warns only the first time
+        warnings.warn(
+            "Could not find the number of physical cores for the "
+            f"following reason:\n{exception}\n"
+            "Returning the number of logical cores instead. You can "
+            "silence this warning by setting LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT to "
+            "the number of cores you want to use.",
+            stacklevel=2
+        )
+        traceback.print_tb(exception.__traceback__)
+
+    return aggregate_cpu_count

Steps to reproduce the change here and in https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238#discussion_r1834424443,

1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.
2. Change your working to `spin` (cloned above).
3. Activate your `scipy` environment. For example I use `scipy-dev` from `conda`. So I do, `conda activate scipy-dev`.
4. Fetch my branch from https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238. I basically do, `git remote add czgdp1807 https://github.com/czgdp1807/spin`. `get fetch czgdp1807 spin_upd`. `czgdp1807` is the remote pointing to my fork.
5. Checkout to `spin_upd` branch (just fetched above).
6. Do an editable install of `spin`. I do, `pip install -e .`.
7. Now switch to SciPy directory in your system.
8. Fetch `spin_build` (this PR) from my fork. Checkout to `spin_build`.
9. Activate the same SciPy environment where you did the editable install of `spin` (in step 6).

1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.
2. Change your working to `spin` (cloned above).

5. Checkout to `spin_upd` branch (just fetched above).
6. Do an editable install of `spin`. I do, `pip install -e .`.
7. Now switch to SciPy directory in your system.
8. Fetch `spin_build` (this PR) from my fork. Checkout to `spin_build`.

+def configure_scipy_openblas(self, blas_variant='32'):
+    """Create scipy-openblas.pc and scipy/_distributor_init_local.py
+
+    Requires a pre-installed scipy-openblas32 wheel from PyPI.
+    """
+    basedir = os.getcwd()

+
+    if os.path.exists(pkg_config_fname):
+        return None
+
+    module_name = f"scipy_openblas{blas_variant}"
+    try:
+        openblas = importlib.import_module(module_name)
+    except ModuleNotFoundError:
+        raise RuntimeError(f"Importing '{module_name}' failed. "
+                            "Make sure it is installed and reachable "
+                            "by the current Python executable. You can "
+                            f"install it via 'pip install {module_name}'.")
+
+    local = os.path.join(basedir, "scipy", "_distributor_init_local.py")
+    with open(local, "w", encoding="utf8") as fid:
+        fid.write(f"import {module_name}\n")
+
+    with open(pkg_config_fname, "w", encoding="utf8") as fid:
+        fid.write(openblas.get_pkg_config())

+def _cpu_count_cgroup(os_cpu_count):
+    # Cgroup CPU bandwidth limit available in Linux since 2.6 kernel
+    cpu_max_fname = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max"
+    cfs_quota_fname = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us"
+    cfs_period_fname = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us"
+    if os.path.exists(cpu_max_fname):
+        # cgroup v2
+        # https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html
+        with open(cpu_max_fname) as fh:
+            cpu_quota_us, cpu_period_us = fh.read().strip().split()
+    elif os.path.exists(cfs_quota_fname) and os.path.exists(cfs_period_fname):
+        # cgroup v1
+        # https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/scheduler/sched-bwc.html#management
+        with open(cfs_quota_fname) as fh:
+            cpu_quota_us = fh.read().strip()
+        with open(cfs_period_fname) as fh:
+            cpu_period_us = fh.read().strip()
+    else:
+        # No Cgroup CPU bandwidth limit (e.g. non-Linux platform)
+        cpu_quota_us = "max"
+        cpu_period_us = 100_000  # unused, for consistency with default values

+    if cpu_quota_us == "max":
+        # No active Cgroup quota on a Cgroup-capable platform
+        return os_cpu_count
+    else:
+        cpu_quota_us = int(cpu_quota_us)
+        cpu_period_us = int(cpu_period_us)
+        if cpu_quota_us > 0 and cpu_period_us > 0:
+            return math.ceil(cpu_quota_us / cpu_period_us)
+        else:  # pragma: no cover

+            # cgroup CPU bandwidth limits

+def _cpu_count_affinity(os_cpu_count):
+    # Number of available CPUs given affinity settings

+        except NotImplementedError:

+    # On PyPy and possibly other platforms, os.sched_getaffinity does not exist
+    # or raises NotImplementedError, let's try with the psutil if installed.
+    try:

+        p = psutil.Process()

+    return os_cpu_count

+def _cpu_count_user(os_cpu_count):

+def _count_physical_cores():
+    """Return a tuple (number of physical cores, exception)
+
+    If the number of physical cores is found, exception is set to None.
+    If it has not been found, return ("not found", exception).

+            cpu_count_physical = len(cpu_info)
+        elif sys.platform == "win32":

+    instead of the number of logical cores (hyperthreading / SMT). Note that

+        # it might be possible to go beyond with a lot of extra work but this

+        os_cpu_count = min(os_cpu_count, _MAX_WINDOWS_WORKERS)
+
+    cpu_count_user = _cpu_count_user(os_cpu_count)

+    if not only_physical_cores:
+        return aggregate_cpu_count

+    if cpu_count_user < os_cpu_count:

Steps to reproduce the change here and in https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238,

1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.
2. Change your working directory to `spin` (cloned above).
3. Activate your `scipy` environment. For example I use `scipy-dev` from `conda`. So I do, `conda activate scipy-dev`.
4. Fetch my branch from https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238. I basically do, `git remote add czgdp1807 https://github.com/czgdp1807/spin`. `get fetch czgdp1807 spin_upd`. `czgdp1807` is the remote pointing to my fork.
5. Checkout to `spin_upd` branch (just fetched above).
6. Do an editable install of `spin`. I do, `pip install -e .`.
7. Now switch to SciPy directory in your system.
8. Fetch `spin_build` (this PR) from my fork. Checkout to `spin_build`.
9. Activate the same SciPy environment where you did the editable install of `spin` (in step 6).

MRE

```fortran
program main
    integer, dimension(2, 2) :: arr
    integer :: dim

    dim = 1
    arr = reshape([1, 2, 3, 4], shape(arr))

    print *, shape(sum(arr, dim))
end program main
```

The `simplifier` pass creates N variables for every N `ArraySize` nodes.

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

In short, this PR adds functionality to generate code coverage report C, C++ and Fortran code in SciPy. Basically achieves the two conditions mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#pullrequestreview-2449299817,

> 1. Run `lcov` in `python dev.py test` only when `--gcov` was enabled during SciPy build.
> 2. Exit without running tests only when any compiler than `gcc` was used to build SciPy and `--gcov` option was enabled. In all other cases run tests as it is.

See my reviews below for explanation behind the changes.

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

In short, this PR adds functionality to generate code coverage report C, C++ and Fortran code in SciPy. Basically achieves the two conditions mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#pullrequestreview-2449299817,

> 1. Run `lcov` in `python dev.py test` only when `--gcov` was enabled during SciPy build.
> 2. Exit without running tests only when any compiler than `gcc` was used to build SciPy and `--gcov` option was enabled. In all other cases run tests as it is.

See my reviews below for explanation behind the changes.

Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/15896

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

In short, this PR adds functionality to generate code coverage report C, C++ and Fortran code in SciPy. Basically achieves the two conditions mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#pullrequestreview-2449299817,

> 1. Run `lcov` in `python dev.py test` only when `--gcov` was enabled during SciPy build.
> 2. Exit without running tests only when any compiler than `gcc` was used to build SciPy and `--gcov` option was enabled. In all other cases run tests as it is.

See my reviews below for explanation behind the changes.

That's why to need to figure out which SciPy build option will go into `setup`, which ones will go into `compile` and which ones will go into `install`. Therefore this segregation can only be done in SciPy. Same can be happen with any other project, they can define their own build options which will map to some `meson` arguments. #### Reference issue
<!--Example: Closes gh-WXYZ.-->

Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/15896

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

In short, this PR adds functionality to generate code coverage report C, C++ and Fortran code in SciPy. Basically achieves the two conditions mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#pullrequestreview-2449299817,

> 1. Run `lcov` in `python dev.py test` only when `--gcov` was enabled during SciPy build.
> 2. Exit without running tests only when any compiler than `gcc` was used to build SciPy and `--gcov` option was enabled. In all other cases run tests as it is.

See my reviews below for explanation behind the changes.

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

The reason for `meson.build:1:0: ERROR: Compiler icx cannot compile programs` https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21934, is due to issues with installing `pythran` and `compilers` from `conda`. Some dependencies of these two conda packages mess up the linker search path i.e., `/usr/lib/gcc` isn't there in the linker search path. So, I have followed the windows way for installing conda packages for this job, i.e., listing minimal set of packages by hand. `pythran` is installed via `pip`. We don't need `compilers` package because we need `icx`, `ifx`, `icpx` which are installed from Intel website.

Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21934

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

The reason for `meson.build:1:0: ERROR: Compiler icx cannot compile programs` https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21934, is due to issues with installing `pythran` and `compilers` from `conda`. Some dependencies of these two conda packages mess up the linker search path i.e., `/usr/lib/gcc` isn't there in the linker search path. So, I have followed the windows way for installing conda packages for this job, i.e., listing minimal set of packages by hand. `pythran` is installed via `pip`. We don't need `compilers` package because we need `icx`, `ifx`, `icpx` which are installed from Intel website.

#### Reference issue

Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21934

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

The reason for `meson.build:1:0: ERROR: Compiler icx cannot compile programs` https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21934, is due to issues with installing `pythran` and `compilers` from `conda`. Some dependencies of these two conda packages mess up the linker search path i.e., `/usr/lib/gcc` isn't there in the linker search path. So, I have followed the windows way for installing conda packages for this job, i.e., listing minimal set of packages by hand. `pythran` is installed via `pip`. We don't need `compilers` package because we need `icx`, `ifx`, `icpx` which are installed from Intel website.

Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21934

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

The reason for `meson.build:1:0: ERROR: Compiler icx cannot compile programs` https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21934, is due to issues with installing `pythran` and `compilers` from `conda`. Some dependencies of these two conda packages mess up the linker search path i.e., `/usr/lib/gcc` isn't there in the linker search path. So, I have followed the windows way for installing conda packages for this job, i.e., listing minimal set of packages by hand. `pythran` is installed via `pip`. We don't need `compilers` package because we need `icx`, `ifx`, `icpx` which are installed from Intel website.

Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21934

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

The reason for `meson.build:1:0: ERROR: Compiler icx cannot compile programs` https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21934, is due to issues with installing `pythran` and `compilers` from `conda`. Some dependencies of these two conda packages mess up the linker search path i.e., `/usr/lib/gcc` isn't there in the linker search path. So, I have followed the windows way for installing conda packages for this job, i.e., listing minimal set of packages by hand. `pythran` is installed via `pip`. We don't need `compilers` package because we need `icx`, `ifx`, `icpx` which are installed from Intel website.

#### Reference issue

Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/15896

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

In short, this PR adds functionality to generate code coverage report C, C++ and Fortran code in SciPy. Basically achieves the two conditions mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#pullrequestreview-2449299817,

> 1. Run `lcov` in `python dev.py test` only when `--gcov` was enabled during SciPy build.
> 2. Exit without running tests only when any compiler than `gcc` was used to build SciPy and `--gcov` option was enabled. In all other cases run tests as it is.

See my reviews below for explanation behind the changes.

In short, this PR adds functionality to generate code coverage report C, C++ and Fortran code in SciPy. Basically achieves the two conditions mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21919#pullrequestreview-2449299817,

> 1. Run `lcov` in `python dev.py test` only when `--gcov` was enabled during SciPy build.
> 2. Exit without running tests only when any compiler than `gcc` was used to build SciPy and `--gcov` option was enabled. In all other cases run tests as it is.

In SciPy each step i.e., `compile`, `setup` and `install` needs arguments from `meson_args`. You can't pass everything from `meson_args` tuple directly into the first command. 1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.
2. Change your working directory to `spin` (cloned above).
3. Activate your `scipy` environment. For example I use `scipy-dev` from `conda`. So I do, `conda activate scipy-dev`.
4. Fetch my branch from https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238. I basically do, `git remote add czgdp1807 https://github.com/czgdp1807/spin`. `get fetch czgdp1807 spin_upd`. `czgdp1807` is the remote pointing to my fork.
5. Checkout to `spin_upd` branch (just fetched above).
6. Do an editable install of `spin`. I do, `pip install -e .`.
7. Now switch to SciPy directory in your system.
8. Fetch `spin_build` (this PR) from my fork. Checkout to `spin_build`.

In SciPy each step i.e., `compile`, `setup` and `install` needs arguments from `meson_args`. You can't pass everything from `meson_args` tuple directly into the first command. So I added 3 keys, `"compile"`, `"setup"` and `"install"` to differentiate which meson argument from SciPy to pass in which step.

However, with my [`meson_kwargs_backup`]() branch of `spin`, where I remove `--destdir` from `meson compile` step. I also specify, `abs_install_dir` for `prefix` in `meson setup` step (see the `diff` below), the tests work on my macOS.

```diff
(scipy-dev-latest) 16:15:56:~/Quansight/spin % git diff meson_kwargs
diff --git a/spin/cmds/meson.py b/spin/cmds/meson.py
index c68273d..b42627e 100644
--- a/spin/cmds/meson.py
+++ b/spin/cmds/meson.py
@@ -335,7 +335,7 @@ def build(
     if gcov:
         meson_args_setup = meson_args_setup + ["-Db_coverage=true"]

-    setup_cmd = _meson_cli() + ["setup", build_dir, f"--prefix={prefix}"] + meson_args_setup
+    setup_cmd = _meson_cli() + ["setup", build_dir, f"--prefix={abs_install_dir}"] + meson_args_setup

     if clean:
         print(f"Removing `{build_dir}`")
@@ -381,10 +381,6 @@ def build(
             "--only-changed",
             "-C",
             build_dir,
-            "--destdir",
-            install_dir
-            if os.path.isabs(install_dir)
-            else os.path.relpath(abs_install_dir, abs_build_dir),
         ] + meson_install_args,
         output=(not quiet) and verbose,
     )
```

On Linux, it works perfectly well with `meson_kwargs` (this branch).

Conclusion - I have to retain my `--destdir` change and `--prefix` change from #238 to make things work with SciPy on my macOS. Writing this comment for our knowledge.

Steps to reproduce the change here and in https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238,

1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.
2. Change your working directory to `spin` (cloned above).
3. Activate your `scipy` environment. For example I use `scipy-dev` from `conda`. So I do, `conda activate scipy-dev`.
4. Fetch my branch from https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/256. I basically do, `git remote add czgdp1807 https://github.com/czgdp1807/spin`. `get fetch czgdp1807 meson_kwargs`. `czgdp1807` is the remote pointing to my fork.
5. Checkout to `meson_kwargs` branch (just fetched above).
6. Do an editable install of `spin`. I do, `pip install -e .`.
7. Now switch to SciPy directory in your system.
8. Fetch `spin_build` (this PR) from my fork. Checkout to `spin_build`.
9. Activate the same SciPy environment where you did the editable install of `spin` (in step 6).

1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.
2. Change your working directory to `spin` (cloned above).
3. Activate your `scipy` environment. For example I use `scipy-dev` from `conda`. So I do, `conda activate scipy-dev`.
4. Fetch my branch from https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/256. I basically do, `git remote add czgdp1807 https://github.com/czgdp1807/spin`. `get fetch czgdp1807 meson_kwargs`. `czgdp1807` is the remote pointing to my fork.
5. Checkout to `meson_kwargs` branch (just fetched above).
6. Do an editable install of `spin`. I do, `pip install -e .`.
7. Now switch to SciPy directory in your system.
8. Fetch `spin_build` (this PR) from my fork. Checkout to `spin_build`.

Steps to reproduce the change here and in https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238,

1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.
2. Change your working directory to `spin` (cloned above).
3. Activate your `scipy` environment. For example I use `scipy-dev` from `conda`. So I do, `conda activate scipy-dev`.
4. Fetch my branch from https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/256. I basically do, `git remote add czgdp1807 https://github.com/czgdp1807/spin`. `get fetch czgdp1807 meson_kwargs`. `czgdp1807` is the remote pointing to my fork.
5. Checkout to `meson_kwargs` branch (just fetched above).
6. Do an editable install of `spin`. I do, `pip install -e .`.
7. Now switch to SciPy directory in your system.
8. Fetch `spin_build` (this PR) from my fork. Checkout to `spin_build`.

Steps to reproduce the change here and in https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238,

1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.
2. Change your working directory to `spin` (cloned above).
3. Activate your `scipy` environment. For example I use `scipy-dev` from `conda`. So I do, `conda activate scipy-dev`.
4. Fetch my branch from https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/256. I basically do, `git remote add czgdp1807 https://github.com/czgdp1807/spin`. `get fetch czgdp1807 meson_kwargs`. `czgdp1807` is the remote pointing to my fork.
5. Checkout to `meson_kwargs` branch (just fetched above).
6. Do an editable install of `spin`. I do, `pip install -e .`.
7. Now switch to SciPy directory in your system.
8. Fetch `spin_build` (this PR) from my fork. Checkout to `spin_build`.
9. Activate the same SciPy environment where you did the editable install of `spin` (in step 6).

Steps to reproduce the change here and in https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/238,

1. Clone `spin` locally into your system. `git clone https://github.com/scientific-python/spin`.
2. Change your working directory to `spin` (cloned above).
3. Activate your `scipy` environment. For example I use `scipy-dev` from `conda`. So I do, `conda activate scipy-dev`.
4. Fetch my branch from https://github.com/scientific-python/spin/pull/256. I basically do, `git remote add czgdp1807 https://github.com/czgdp1807/spin`. `get fetch czgdp1807 meson_kwargs`. `czgdp1807` is the remote pointing to my fork.
5. Checkout to `meson_kwargs` branch (just fetched above).
6. Do an editable install of `spin`. I do, `pip install -e .`.
7. Now switch to SciPy directory in your system.
8. Fetch `spin_build` (this PR) from my fork. Checkout to `spin_build`.
